subject: dsp
title: Systems, Convolution and Filters
summary: Predict how systems transform samples, design simple FIR and IIR filters, and preserve their behaviour across processing blocks.

lessons.title: Two tests for a predictable system
lessons.summary: Test linearity and time invariance, and understand why initial state belongs in the assumptions.
lessons.body:
A **discrete-time system** takes an input sequence and produces an output sequence. Multiplying every sensor reading by two is a system. So is smoothing several readings or clipping values above a limit. Before choosing a filter, ask which mathematical shortcuts its behaviour permits.

## Linearity means preserving combinations

A **linear system** preserves scaling and addition together. Processing a mixture must give the same result as processing its components separately and then mixing their outputs with the same weights. This property is **superposition**. It must hold for every allowed pair of inputs and every allowed constant weight; one successful example cannot prove it.

Here is the test written compactly. The letters representing sequences mean whole sequences, rather than individual samples.

```formula
T(ax + bv) = aT(x) + bT(v)
where
T: the system operation, mapping an entire input sequence to an output sequence
x: the first input sequence, with dimensionless sample values in this example
v: the second input sequence, in the same dimensionless units as x
a: a constant dimensionless weight for the first sequence
b: a constant dimensionless weight for the second sequence
In words: combining weighted inputs before processing must match combining the separately processed outputs with those same weights.
```

Doubling every reading passes this test. Squaring does not: a reading of 2 produces 4, while doubling the input produces 16 rather than doubling the output to 8. Adding a constant offset of 1 also fails: zero input produces a nonzero output. Zero input producing zero output is necessary for linearity, though it is not a sufficient test by itself.

## Time invariance means the same rule later

A **time-invariant system** gives an equally shifted output when its entire input is shifted. A fixed one-sample delay passes: sending a pulse three samples later moves the delayed pulse three samples later too. Multiplying each sample by its absolute sample index fails: an identical pulse gets a different gain when it arrives later.

Linearity and time invariance are separate tests. A fixed squaring operation is time invariant but nonlinear. Multiplication by the sample index is linear but time varying. A system that passes both is **linear time-invariant**, or **LTI**. Fixed weighted sums of present and past inputs are important examples.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: an unchanged recipe
> Doubling two ingredients and combining batches works predictably when the recipe scales consistently. Preparing the same batch tomorrow should also give the same result.
>
> **How it maps:** Scaling and combining batches suggest linearity; applying the same recipe on a later day suggests time invariance.
>
> **Where it stops:** Real cooking is rarely linear. Temperature, vessel size and chemical changes can break both predictions.

## Include the initial state

Filters may remember earlier samples. **Zero state** means their stored history is initially zero. An input/output linearity test must include that assumption: a filter already holding a nonzero output can respond even to zero new input.

For time-shift comparisons, shift the complete input history and use the corresponding zero-state setup. Restarting a device midway through one run changes the experiment. Likewise, finite-array truncation can hide a delayed output; compare the whole relevant output, including its tail.

## Key takeaways
- Linearity preserves weighted combinations; time invariance preserves shifts.
- One counterexample disproves either property.
- State and record boundaries must be part of an LTI claim.

## Further reading
- [Smith: linear systems, Chapter 5](https://www.dspguide.com/CH5.PDF)
- [Julius O. Smith: LTI digital filters](https://www.dsprelated.com/freebooks/filters/Linear_Time_Invariant_Digital_Filters.html)

questions.prompt: A system adds 1 to every input sample. Which observation disproves linearity?

options.text: Every output arrives at the same time as its input
options.explanation: Timing alone does not establish or disprove preservation of weighted combinations.

options.text: An all-zero input produces an all-one output
options.explanation: Correct. A linear zero-state input/output mapping must map zero input to zero output.

options.text: A later input gets the same offset
options.explanation: That is consistent with time invariance, which is a separate property from linearity.

options.text: Negative inputs are accepted
options.explanation: Accepting negative values does not show how their combinations are processed.

questions.workedExample:
1. Consider an all-zero sequence.
2. Multiplying it by any constant leaves it unchanged.
3. A linear system must preserve that scaling, which forces its output for zero input to be zero.
4. The fixed added offset produces ones instead, so one counterexample is enough to reject linearity.

questions.prompt: A system multiplies each reading by its absolute sample index. A unit pulse at index 2 produces amplitude 2; the same pulse at index 5 produces amplitude 5. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: It is time invariant because both pulses remain pulses
options.explanation: Time invariance requires the same output shape and amplitude shifted in time, not merely the same general signal type.

options.text: It must be nonlinear
options.explanation: A predetermined index-dependent multiplier still preserves scaling and addition.

options.text: It fails time invariance
options.explanation: Correct. Moving the input pulse changes the output amplitude as well as its position.

options.text: One must measure infinitely many pulses first
options.explanation: A single valid counterexample is sufficient to disprove time invariance.

questions.workedExample:
1. Delay the original pulse by three samples.
2. Time invariance would require the original amplitude-2 output to move three samples later unchanged.
3. The actual delayed experiment produces amplitude 5.
4. The disagreement disproves time invariance, even though the system is linear.

lessons.title: Learn a system from one impulse
lessons.summary: Use an isolated unit impulse to reveal an LTI system's weights, memory and causality.
lessons.body:
A **unit impulse** is a discrete sequence containing 1 at sample zero and 0 everywhere else, including negative sample indices. It is a single nonzero sample, rather than a narrow continuous-time spike of unspecified height.

The **impulse response** is the output produced by this input when a system starts at rest. For an LTI system, it tells us how every input sample contributes to future output. Each sample can be viewed as its own scaled, shifted impulse. Linearity lets us add their responses; time invariance lets us shift the same response to each arrival time.

## Reveal the weights

Consider a system that combines the present sample and the previous one. All input values before sample zero are zero.

```formula
y[n] = 0.75x[n] + 0.25x[n − 1]
where
y: the output sequence, with dimensionless sample values
x: the input sequence, with dimensionless sample values
n: the integer sample index; n starts at zero for this record
0.75: the dimensionless weight on the present input
0.25: the dimensionless weight on the previous input
In words: each output is three quarters of the current reading plus one quarter of the previous reading.
```

The impulse produces 0.75 at sample zero, 0.25 at sample one, then zeros. That two-sample response exposes the two weights directly. A pulse with amplitude 4 produces 3, then 1. A pulse arriving five samples later produces that same pair five samples later. The output depends on both the pulse and what the system remembers, so the system must start in zero state for this interpretation.

This complete Python example uses a list for the input and one variable for its remembered previous sample. It prints the first four response values.

```python
x = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
previous = 0.0
y = []
for sample in x:
    y.append(0.75*sample + 0.25*previous)
    previous = sample
print(y)
# [0.75, 0.25, 0.0, 0.0]
```

## Causality is about available information

A **causal system** uses only present and past inputs. For a zero-state LTI system this means its impulse response is zero at every negative sample index. It cannot produce a response before the impulse arrives. A filter that needs tomorrow's sensor reading is noncausal in a live stream, although a saved recording may make that future sample available for offline processing.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a single clap
> A clap in a room is followed by reflections that become quieter over time.
>
> **How it maps:** The isolated event is the test input; the sequence of reflections suggests how a system can spread one event through time.
>
> **Where it stops:** A clap is not an exact discrete unit impulse, and a real room measurement includes the microphone, source and background noise. It does not prove the room is LTI.

## What one experiment cannot establish

An impulse response fully characterises an already established LTI system under its initial-state assumptions. It does not prove an unknown system is linear or time invariant. A clipper may look like an unchanged connection for a small impulse yet distort larger signals. A changing system may respond differently tomorrow. A short measurement can also miss a long, quiet tail.

## Key takeaways
- A discrete unit impulse has one sample of amplitude 1 and zeros elsewhere.
- Its zero-state response characterises an LTI system.
- Causality excludes response before the input; one test cannot prove LTI behaviour.

## Further reading
- [Julius O. Smith: impulse-response representation](https://www.dsprelated.com/freebooks/filters/Impulse_Response_Representation.html)
- [Smith: convolution and impulse responses, Chapter 6](https://www.dspguide.com/CH6.PDF)

questions.prompt: A zero-state filter outputs three quarters of the present input plus one quarter of the previous input. What are the first three outputs for a unit impulse at sample zero?

options.explanation: Correct. The impulse contributes through the present-input weight, then the previous-input weight, then neither.
That resembles a sustained response, but this filter only uses two input positions.
The present-input term acts immediately; there is no additional one-sample delay.
This repeats the first weight rather than shifting the single impulse through the input history.

questions.workedExample:
At the first output only the present input is nonzero. At the second, only the previous input is nonzero. Afterwards both inputs are zero.

```formula
y_0 = 0.75 × 1 + 0.25 × 0 = 0.75
y_1 = 0.75 × 0 + 0.25 × 1 = 0.25
y_2 = 0.75 × 0 + 0.25 × 0 = 0
where
y_0: dimensionless output at sample zero
y_1: dimensionless output at sample one
y_2: dimensionless output at sample two
In words: the isolated input reveals each weight in order.
```

questions.prompt: A zero-state LTI filter has a nonzero impulse-response sample before the input impulse arrives. What does that say about the model?

options.text: It must amplify every input
options.explanation: Pre-response is about timing and causality, not overall gain.

options.text: It must be unstable
options.explanation: A finite response before the impulse does not imply unbounded output.

options.text: It cannot process a saved recording
options.explanation: Offline processing can use future samples available in a recording.

options.text: It is noncausal
options.explanation: Correct. A causal zero-state LTI system cannot respond before the impulse arrives.

questions.workedExample:
1. Before the impulse, the input history contains only zeros.
2. A causal zero-state LTI system has no information from future samples.
3. A nonzero pre-response therefore requires a noncausal model.
4. Such a model may still be usable offline, where later samples have already been recorded.

questions.prompt: An unknown device reproduces one small test impulse perfectly. Which conclusions are justified? Select all that apply.

options.text: Every large input will also be reproduced perfectly
options.explanation: A clipper can preserve a small impulse yet distort larger values.

options.text: This test records its response for these conditions
options.explanation: Correct. The experiment measures a particular input, initial state and operating condition.

options.text: More testing is needed before claiming it is LTI
options.explanation: Correct. One impulse experiment does not establish linearity and time invariance.

options.text: Any unobserved tail is exactly zero
options.explanation: A finite measurement can miss a long or quiet response tail.

questions.workedExample:
1. Record what was actually measured: a small pulse under one setup.
2. Consider a device that clips only larger inputs; it could pass this experiment.
3. Consider a device whose coefficients change later; it could also pass now.
4. An impulse response characterises an established LTI model, while this one test alone cannot establish that model.

lessons.title: Convolution as overlapping contributions
lessons.summary: Compute finite linear convolution, including zero extension and the output tail.
lessons.body:
**Linear convolution** combines an input with an impulse response to predict the output of a zero-state LTI system. Each input sample launches a scaled copy of the response. When copies overlap, add their contributions. Unlike correlation, convolution models a system's response; it is not a template-similarity score.

## First add the copies

Take input `[2, 1, 3]` and impulse response `[1, 0.5]`, both starting at sample zero. The first input launches `[2, 1]`. The next launches `[1, 0.5]` one sample later. The third launches `[3, 1.5]` two samples later. Adding aligned entries produces `[2, 2, 3.5, 1.5]`.

The last output remains after the final nonzero input. That **filter tail** is part of full convolution. This is linear convolution with zero extension: values outside either stored sequence are treated as zero. There is no wrapping from one end of an array to the other.

## Then write the weighted sum

The capital Greek letter sigma means “add the following terms”. The lower limit starts the counter at zero; the upper limit includes the last coefficient. The counter changes inside the sum while the output index stays fixed.

```formula
y[n] = Σ_{k=0}^{M−1} h[k]x[n − k]
L = N + M − 1
where
y: the output sequence, with dimensionless sample values here
x: the input sequence of N samples; zero outside indices zero through N minus one
h: the impulse response of M dimensionless coefficients; zero outside indices zero through M minus one
n: the output sample index, from zero through L minus one
k: the integer coefficient index, counting from zero through M minus one
M: the positive integer number of impulse-response coefficients
N: the positive integer number of input samples
L: the number of samples in the full output array, including its tail
Σ_{k=0}^{M−1}: finite summation; evaluate the following product for each integer k from zero through M minus one and add the results
In words: multiply each response weight by the appropriately delayed input, add the contributions, and keep enough output samples for every overlap.
```

Some final output values may happen to be zero; the length formula describes the full array, not the number of nonzero results. For three input samples and two weights it gives four output positions. At output sample two, the present input contributes 3 and the previous input contributes 0.5.

## Implement the input-side view

This complete example starts an all-zero output and adds one shifted response for each input sample. Python `enumerate` supplies each index alongside its value.

```python
x = [2.0, 1.0, 3.0]
h = [1.0, 0.5]
y = [0.0] * (len(x) + len(h) - 1)
for i, sample in enumerate(x):
    for k, weight in enumerate(h):
        y[i + k] += sample * weight
print(y)
# [2.0, 2.0, 3.5, 1.5]
```

NumPy's `convolve` with `mode="full"` computes this discrete linear convolution for one-dimensional arrays. Other modes select fewer output positions; they do not create a physically different filter. Always choose which part of the full result your application needs. In particular, “same” length is an array-selection policy, not a guarantee of causal alignment.

## Key takeaways
- Convolution adds shifted, scaled impulse responses.
- Finite linear convolution uses zeros beyond the records and preserves a tail.
- State the output mode and alignment whenever comparing implementations.

## Further reading
- [Smith: convolution, Chapter 6](https://www.dspguide.com/CH6.PDF)
- [NumPy: convolve and its boundary modes](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.convolve.html)

questions.prompt: An input record has 4 samples and a finite impulse response has 3 coefficients. How many positions are in their full linear convolution?

options.explanation: That could be a selected output length, but it omits positions in the complete response tail.
There are twelve input-weight products, but products overlap in output positions.
Correct. Full convolution includes the original span and two additional output positions for its tail.
Adding the two lengths without subtracting one counts the shared starting position twice.

questions.workedExample:
Both records start at sample zero and are zero elsewhere.

```formula
L = N + M − 1
L = 4 + 3 − 1 = 6
where
L: full output-array length in samples
N: input-array length, here four samples
M: impulse-response length, here three coefficients
In words: the final input can launch a three-position response, extending the output by two positions.
```

Some values can happen to be zero, but that does not change this full array length.

questions.prompt: Input `[2, 1, 3]` is convolved with weights `[1, 0.5]`, with zero extension. What is output sample 2, counting the first sample as index zero?

options.explanation: Correct. The present input contributes 3 and the previous input contributes 0.5.
That is the final tail value, after the present input has become zero.
That is output sample one, not output sample two.
This incorrectly gives the previous input a full weight of one.

questions.workedExample:
At sample two, align the first coefficient with the present input and the second with the previous input.

```formula
y[2] = 1 × 3 + 0.5 × 1 = 3.5
where
y: the output sequence, with dimensionless sample values
2: the output index, counting from zero
In words: the current reading contributes three and the preceding reading contributes one half.
```

The full output is `[2, 2, 3.5, 1.5]`.

questions.prompt: Two programs use the same input and weights, but one requests full convolution and the other requests a same-length selection. Why can their arrays have different lengths without their weighted-sum calculation disagreeing?

options.text: Same-length mode must use feedback
options.explanation: Output selection does not turn a feedforward convolution into a feedback recurrence.

options.text: Full mode wraps the end around
options.explanation: Full linear convolution uses zero extension; it does not wrap.

options.text: Only the shorter output can be causal
options.explanation: Causality and indexing require inspecting alignment, not merely the output length.

options.text: They retain different positions from the full result
options.explanation: Correct. Boundary mode can select a subset of the same underlying linear-convolution result.

questions.workedExample:
1. Compute the complete zero-extended weighted-sum output, including its tail.
2. A shorter output mode keeps only specified positions.
3. Compare matching indices rather than assuming the first stored positions refer to the same time.
4. In particular, a same-length API result does not by itself establish causal alignment.

lessons.title: Smooth a stream with a moving average
lessons.summary: Build a causal moving average and distinguish smoothing, startup effects and delay.
lessons.body:
A **moving average** gives equal weight to a fixed number of neighbouring samples. It can reduce rapid fluctuations when the useful quantity changes slowly. For a live sensor stream, choose present and past samples so the operation is causal. A centred average on a saved recording is a different timing choice because it also uses future samples.

## A three-sample average

This causal version includes the present reading and two older ones. It starts with zero history, and its divisor stays three even during startup.

```formula
y[n] = (x[n] + x[n − 1] + x[n − 2]) / 3
where
y: the smoothed output sequence, in the same units as the input
x: the input sequence; samples before index zero are zero
n: the integer sample index, starting at zero
3: the number of equally weighted samples in this average, including zero history during startup
In words: add the current reading and the two previous readings, then divide by three.
```

Suppose a sensor suddenly changes from zero to 6 and stays there. The first outputs are 2, 4 and 6. The filter needs three nonzero input samples to fill its window. This **startup transient** follows from the declared zero history; it is not a calculation error.

A program that instead divides the first sum by one and the second by two outputs 6 immediately. That may be a useful boundary policy, but it is not the same fixed-coefficient LTI filter at the beginning of the record. Initialising past samples to the first reading also changes the initial state.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a three-day spending average
> A daily dashboard averages today's spending with the previous two days. One expensive day affects three successive dashboard entries.
>
> **How it maps:** The sliding set of days maps to the filter's sample window; equal shares map to equal coefficients. A sharp event spreads across several outputs.
>
> **Where it stops:** Days without records are often omitted in a dashboard. This filter explicitly fills missing earlier history with zeros and keeps its divisor fixed.

## Smoothness has a timing cost

The three coefficients are symmetric, so this filter has a linear phase response and a group delay of one sample wherever its frequency response is nonzero. Group delay describes how the phase changes across a small frequency interval. It does not mean every output sample is simply the input shifted by one place: smoothing changes amplitudes and shapes, and response sign changes can add phase jumps.

At 100 samples per second, one sample is 0.01 seconds. An abrupt event spreads across three output samples. For an alarm, that spreading can matter more than how quiet the line looks on a plot. A longer average generally smooths more rapid variation and spreads a change over more samples.

Complete Python example: NumPy is imported as `np`, and `convolve` includes the tail after the four input samples. The first four outputs are the causal outputs while readings arrive; the remaining two come from feeding zero input afterwards.

```python
import numpy as np

x = [6.0, 6.0, 6.0, 6.0]
h = np.ones(3) / 3
y = np.convolve(x, h, mode="full")
print(y.tolist())
# [2.0, 4.0, 6.0, 6.0, 4.0, 2.0]
```

## Key takeaways
- A causal moving average uses present and past readings.
- Zero history and a fixed divisor create a predictable startup transient.
- Smoothing changes amplitudes and timing; choose the window for the task.

## Further reading
- [Smith: moving average filters, Chapter 15](https://www.dspguide.com/CH15.PDF)
- [Julius O. Smith: symmetric linear-phase filters](https://www.dsprelated.com/freebooks/filters/Symmetric_Linear_Phase_Filters.html)

questions.prompt: A causal three-sample moving average starts with zero history and always divides by three. The input steps from zero to 6. What are its first three outputs?

options.explanation: That would require a different startup policy, such as dividing by the number of available samples.
Correct. One, then two, then three nonzero readings fill the fixed three-position window.
A moving average produces partial outputs during startup; it need not wait until its whole window is nonzero.
The previous nonzero inputs remain in the window and contribute to later outputs.

questions.workedExample:
Keep the declared zero history and fixed divisor.

```formula
y_0 = (6 + 0 + 0) / 3 = 2
y_1 = (6 + 6 + 0) / 3 = 4
y_2 = (6 + 6 + 6) / 3 = 6
where
y_0: dimensionless output at sample zero
y_1: dimensionless output at sample one
y_2: dimensionless output at sample two
In words: the average rises as the step fills the window.
```

questions.prompt: A programmer divides the first moving-average sum by one, the second by two and later sums by three. How should this be described?

options.text: The same zero-state fixed three-tap filter
options.explanation: The changing divisor changes the early weights, so the input/output rule differs at startup.

options.text: An unavoidable floating-point error
options.explanation: This is a deliberate boundary-policy change rather than a representation error.

options.text: A different startup boundary policy
options.explanation: Correct. Averaging only the available readings may be useful, but it differs from fixed coefficients with zero history.

options.text: A guarantee of zero phase shift at every frequency
options.explanation: Changing the startup divisor does not establish a steady-state phase response or remove the causal window's delay.

questions.workedExample:
1. Compare the first output for a reading of 6.
2. The fixed three-position average outputs 2 because two history positions contain zeros.
3. The available-readings average outputs 6 because it divides by one.
4. Both can be intentionally chosen, but they are different operations and should not be compared as identical LTI implementations.

questions.prompt: A three-tap equal-weight causal average runs at 100 samples per second. Its group delay is one sample where the response is nonzero. What is that delay in seconds?

options.text: 0.01 seconds
options.explanation: Correct. One sample interval at this rate is one hundredth of a second.

options.text: 1 second
options.explanation: This mistakes a sample interval for a whole second.

options.text: 0 seconds because the coefficients are symmetric
options.explanation: Symmetry gives a known linear-phase delay for the causal filter, not zero delay.

options.text: 0.03 seconds
options.explanation: Three sample intervals describe the window's length in intervals, not this filter's one-sample group delay.

questions.workedExample:
Convert the given sample delay using the sample rate.

```formula
τ = D / F_s
τ = 1 / (100 s^{−1}) = 0.01 s
where
τ: group delay in seconds (s)
D: delay of one sample interval
F_s: sample rate of 100 sample intervals per second
s: second; s to the power minus one means per second
In words: at one hundred samples per second, one sample interval lasts one hundredth of a second.
```

This does not mean the entire output is an unchanged delayed copy: the average also changes amplitudes.

link.title: Julius O. Smith: symmetric linear-phase filters

lessons.title: What happens to each frequency?
lessons.summary: Interpret steady-state gain and phase, and turn a vague smoothing goal into frequency requirements.
lessons.body:
A filter can preserve a slowly varying trend while reducing faster oscillations. Its **frequency response** describes how a stable LTI system scales and shifts sinusoids at each frequency after startup effects have passed. **Amplitude response** gives the amplitude ratio; **phase response** gives the phase shift. A negative output value at one instant is not a negative amplitude ratio: amplitude ratios are nonnegative.

For a sinusoid present long enough for steady behaviour and a nonzero output amplitude, the following description applies. It uses radians for phase and hertz for frequency. At a response zero the output is zero and its phase is undefined; exclude that case from the phase-bearing expression below.

```formula
x[n] = A cos(2πfn / F_s + φ)
y[n] = AG cos(2πfn / F_s + φ + θ)
where
x: the sinusoidal input sequence, with dimensionless sample values
y: the steady-state output sequence, in the same dimensionless units
n: the integer sample index of the ideal continuing steady-state sinusoid
A: the positive input peak amplitude, dimensionless here
G: the positive amplitude gain at the chosen frequency, dimensionless; the zero-gain case is excluded from this expression
f: the sinusoid frequency in hertz (Hz), below half the sample rate
F_s: the sample rate in samples per second
φ: the input phase in radians
θ: the filter's phase shift at this frequency, in radians
π: pi, approximately 3.14159
cos: the cosine function, taking an angle in radians
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: an LTI filter keeps a steady sinusoid's frequency while changing its amplitude and phase.
```

## Measure a simple response

A two-sample moving average has gain 1 for constant input. At a quarter of the sample rate, its gain is about 0.707 and its phase shift is minus a quarter of pi radians. At half the sample rate, alternating 1 and minus 1 cancel exactly once the history is filled. These different outcomes are the same filter acting on different frequencies.

The complete example checks the quarter-rate tone after startup. Here `arange` creates integer sample indices and `cos` acts on every array element. The direct expression for the expected output uses the predicted amplitude and half-sample delay. `allclose` compares arrays allowing small floating-point rounding errors.

```python
import numpy as np

n = np.arange(12)
x = np.cos(np.pi*n/2)
y = np.convolve(x, [0.5, 0.5])
expected = np.cos(np.pi*(n-0.5)/2)
expected *= np.sqrt(0.5)
assert np.allclose(y[1:12], expected[1:])
```

## Specify useful and unwanted bands

The **passband** is the frequency region intended to pass within a specified gain tolerance. The **stopband** is intended to be sufficiently reduced. The **transition band** lies between them. A **low-pass filter** passes low frequencies and reduces higher ones, but no finite filter here makes an instantaneous jump between perfect passage and perfect rejection.

For a 100-sample-per-second sensor, an illustrative requirement might preserve 0–2 Hz within a chosen tolerance and strongly reduce frequencies above 15 Hz. The tolerated gain error and required reduction must also be stated before deciding whether a design succeeds.

A moving average has cancellation frequencies but also unwanted lobes between them. Increasing its length does not turn it into a universal frequency separator. It also cannot recover information already lost to aliasing, and it reduces useful signal components occupying the same frequencies as unwanted noise. Define the task before choosing the filter.

## Key takeaways
- Stable LTI filtering changes steady-state sinusoidal amplitude and phase, not frequency.
- Startup behaviour must be excluded or modelled when measuring response.
- Passband, stopband, tolerances and timing requirements guide filter choice.

## Further reading
- [Julius O. Smith: frequency response](https://www.dsprelated.com/freebooks/filters/Frequency_Response.html)
- [Julius O. Smith: steady sinusoidal response](https://www.dsprelated.com/freebooks/filters/Introduction_I_I.html)
- [Smith: moving average frequency behaviour, Chapter 15](https://www.dspguide.com/CH15.PDF)

questions.prompt: A stable LTI filter receives a 7 Hz sinusoid. After startup, its nonzero output has half the input amplitude and a phase shift. What frequency does the output sinusoid have?

options.text: 3.5 Hz
options.explanation: Halving amplitude does not halve frequency.

options.text: 14 Hz
options.explanation: A stable LTI response does not double a steady sinusoid's frequency.

options.text: 0 Hz
options.explanation: A phase shift does not turn an oscillation into a constant signal.

options.text: 7 Hz
options.explanation: Correct. Steady sinusoidal frequency is preserved while amplitude and phase change.

lessons.title: Design and inspect a small FIR filter
lessons.summary: Design a low-pass FIR, check its actual response, and account for symmetric-filter delay.
lessons.body:
A **finite impulse response**, or **FIR**, filter has an impulse response that becomes exactly zero after a finite number of samples. A direct FIR implementation multiplies present and past inputs by fixed **filter coefficients** and adds them. Each coefficient is often called an **FIR tap**. A moving average is an FIR with equal taps; useful FIR filters need not use equal or positive coefficients.

## Ask a design tool a precise question

SciPy's `signal.firwin` designs FIR coefficients using the **window method**: it limits and shapes an ideal response's coefficient sequence. The details of window choices come later. Here we request 31 taps, a Hamming window, a low-pass response, and an explicit sample rate of 100 samples per second.

The `cutoff` of 10 Hz is this API's half-amplitude point, approximately minus 6 dB, rather than a promise that every frequency below 10 Hz has gain 1. `scale=True` normalises this low-pass design to unity gain at DC. Always check an API's convention before treating a parameter as a passband edge.

This complete example measures the returned coefficients using `freqz`. Its frequency argument is a one-dimensional array of frequencies in hertz because `fs` is supplied. `abs` obtains the magnitude of the complex response; `round` only formats the printed values.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import signal

b = signal.firwin(
    31, 10, fs=100, window="hamming",
    pass_zero="lowpass", scale=True)
f = np.array([0.0, 5.0, 10.0, 25.0])
_, response = signal.freqz(b, worN=f,
                         fs=100)
print(np.round(abs(response), 6).tolist())
# [1.0, 0.989021, 0.498204, 5e-06]
assert np.allclose(b, b[::-1])
```

The last displayed value means five millionths after rounding, rather than an exact zero. These are four response checks, not proof that an entire band meets a tolerance. A real specification needs a sufficiently thorough frequency-grid check and attention to extrema between grid points. Increasing the tap count with a comparable window usually narrows the transition, while window choice trades transition width against residual **filter ripple** and stopband attenuation. More taps also mean more work and, for this symmetric design, more delay.

## Symmetry gives a specific delay

Real, symmetric FIR coefficients give linear phase. Their **group delay** is constant wherever the response is nonzero and the phase can be followed continuously. The gain may change sign in the corresponding zero-phase response, causing phase jumps; phase is undefined at exact response zeros.

```formula
D = (M − 1) / 2
τ = D / F_s
D = (31 − 1) / 2 = 15
τ = 15 / (100 s^{−1}) = 0.15 s
where
D: the group delay in sample intervals for a causal real symmetric FIR with nonzero response at the frequency considered
M: the number of coefficients, here 31
τ: the corresponding delay in seconds (s)
F_s: the sample rate in sample intervals per second, here 100
s: second, the unit of time; s to the power minus one means per second
In words: the centre of a symmetric 31-tap causal FIR lies 15 sample intervals behind its newest input, giving 0.15 seconds at this sample rate.
```

An even number of symmetric taps gives a half-integer delay in sample intervals, which is valid. Arbitrary FIR coefficients need not have constant group delay. Nor does “FIR” mean “zero delay”. Shifting a saved output backwards can align a recording, but cannot make future samples available to a live system or undo changed amplitudes. Startup and the finite tail still need a policy.

## Key takeaways
- FIR taps describe finite memory; a design parameter needs an API convention.
- Inspect response, including transition and ripple, against actual requirements.
- Real symmetric FIRs have a known group delay where their response is nonzero.

## Further reading
- [SciPy: firwin design and cutoff convention](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.firwin.html)
- [SciPy: freqz response evaluation](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.freqz.html)
- [Julius O. Smith: symmetric linear-phase filters](https://www.dsprelated.com/freebooks/filters/Symmetric_Linear_Phase_Filters.html)

lessons.title: A smoother that remembers its output
lessons.summary: Trace a one-pole feedback smoother and distinguish stored state from an FIR's finite history.
lessons.body:
**Feedforward paths** use present or previous inputs. **Feedback paths** use previous outputs. With feedback, an input's influence can be passed forward repeatedly rather than ending after a fixed number of taps. An **infinite impulse response**, or **IIR**, filter can therefore have a theoretically endless impulse-response tail, even when that tail becomes extremely small.

## Mix a new reading with the old result

A **one-pole smoother** keeps one previous output. Here the coefficient names follow an explicit convention: the memory weight is on the previous output, and the complementary weight is on the current input.

```formula
y[n] = (1 − a)x[n] + ay[n − 1]
0 < a < 1
where
y: the output sequence, with dimensionless sample values here; its value at index minus one is initially zero
x: the input sequence, with dimensionless sample values
n: the integer sample index, starting at zero
a: the dimensionless memory weight on the previous output; larger values in this range retain history longer
In words: take part of the new reading and part of the previous output, with weights that add to one.
```

With a memory weight of 0.5, a step from zero to 1 produces 0.5, 0.75, 0.875 and 0.9375. Each output closes half the remaining gap. It approaches 1 but does not reach it in a finite number of steps in exact arithmetic. A memory weight of 0.9 responds more slowly than 0.5; its first output is only 0.1 from zero state.

For an isolated unit impulse and memory weight 0.5, the outputs are 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 and so on. The decreasing tail explains the IIR name. A real computer eventually rounds very small changes away or encounters its representation limits; “infinite” describes the mathematical response, not an infinite array stored in memory.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a slowly updated estimate
> A person revises an estimate halfway towards each new observation rather than replacing it immediately.
>
> **How it maps:** The old estimate maps to the previous output; the new observation maps to the current input. Repeated partial updates retain past information with decreasing influence.
>
> **Where it stops:** A person may change their judgement rules. This filter uses fixed numerical weights, and its state is exactly specified.

## Implement the remembered value

Complete Python example: `state` holds the previous output and is updated after every input. This is the whole persistent state for this particular implementation.

```python
x = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
a = 0.5
state = 0.0
y = []
for sample in x:
    state = (1-a)*sample + a*state
    y.append(state)
print(y)
# [0.5, 0.75, 0.875, 0.9375]
```

SciPy's `lfilter` uses denominator coefficients with a subtraction convention. This same smoother is represented by numerator `[0.5]` and denominator `[1.0, -0.5]`. Copying a positive memory weight into the denominator without changing its sign gives a different filter. Other authors may call the current-input weight “alpha”; compare the recurrence, not just the name.

This smoother needs little state, but its phase delay generally varies with frequency. Choosing IIR over a symmetric FIR changes more than coefficient count. Stability and numerical precision need separate attention next.

## Key takeaways
- Feedback reuses earlier outputs; a decaying influence can continue indefinitely.
- Name which weight multiplies which value before comparing coefficients.
- Resetting the remembered output changes the signal being computed.

## Further reading
- [Julius O. Smith: the one-pole filter](https://www.dsprelated.com/freebooks/filters/One_Pole.html)
- [SciPy: lfilter coefficient and state conventions](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.lfilter.html)

lessons.title: Stability and numerical limits
lessons.summary: Separate bounded-output mathematics from overflow, coefficient rounding and finite test evidence.
lessons.body:
**Bounded-input bounded-output stability**, or **BIBO stability**, means every bounded input produces a bounded output for the stated system and initial conditions. “Bounded” means there is a finite ceiling on absolute magnitude for all time; it does not mean “small enough for this particular computer type”. Here we analyse causal filters in zero state with exact arithmetic first.

## Why the convex smoother stays bounded

The previous lesson's smoother uses positive weights that add to one. If the new reading and previous output both lie within a fixed magnitude bound, their weighted average stays inside it too.

```formula
y[n] = (1 − a)x[n] + ay[n − 1]
0 ≤ a < 1
|x[n]| ≤ B
|y[n − 1]| ≤ B
|y[n]| ≤ (1 − a)B + aB = B
where
y: the output sequence, with dimensionless sample values; zero initial state satisfies the bound
x: the input sequence, with dimensionless sample values
n: the integer sample index, starting at zero; the previous output before the record is zero
a: the dimensionless previous-output weight in the stated range
B: a finite nonnegative magnitude bound, in the same dimensionless units as the samples
| |: absolute value, the nonnegative magnitude of a real number
≤: less than or equal to
In words: a weighted average of two readings inside the bound stays inside the bound, so the argument continues sample after sample.
```

This proves a useful property for this specific normalised smoother. Negative feedback coefficients require a different magnitude argument. A fixed FIR with finitely many finite coefficients is also BIBO stable: each output adds only a fixed finite number of bounded contributions.

## A one-pole condition, with its scope

For the following different recurrence, the input weight is fixed at 1. Its **filter pole** is the memory multiplier: an existing disturbance is repeatedly multiplied by it. This beginner example avoids needing a general pole-zero calculation.

```formula
y[n] = x[n] + py[n − 1]
|p| < 1
where
y: the causal output sequence in zero initial state, with dimensionless samples
x: the input sequence, with dimensionless samples and input weight fixed at one
n: the integer sample index, starting at zero; the previous output before the record is zero
p: the real dimensionless memory multiplier and the pole of this specific recurrence
| |: absolute value, ignoring the sign of the real multiplier
<: strictly less than
In words: this one-pole filter is BIBO stable exactly when the magnitude of its memory multiplier is below one.
```

With a multiplier of 0.5, an impulse produces 1, 0.5, 0.25 and progressively smaller values. With 1, a constant input of 1 produces 1, 2, 3 and unbounded growth. With minus 1, an alternating bounded input can likewise make the magnitude grow. A finite test that happens to look quiet cannot prove stability for every bounded input.

## The computer is a separate constraint

**Numerical overflow** occurs when a result exceeds a representation's range. A stable filter with gain 100 can still overflow a narrow integer type when a large bounded input arrives. **Rounding error** occurs because many values have no exact finite representation. Rounding coefficients can also change the implemented filter, so check its actual stored coefficients, especially near a stability boundary.

This complete example deliberately uses signed 16-bit integer array arithmetic. It shows overflow in a simple gain operation, not a complete fixed-point filter implementation.

```python
import numpy as np

x = np.array([20000], dtype=np.int16)
y = x * np.int16(2)
print(y.tolist())
# [-25536]
```

Use suitable types, scaling, numerical range validation and representative stress inputs. Floating-point arithmetic also has finite precision and range. SciPy recommends second-order-section filtering for most general IIR tasks because it reduces numerical problems; our one-state example does not establish safety for high-order direct forms.

## Key takeaways
- Mathematical stability concerns all bounded inputs over unlimited time.
- The stated one-pole condition belongs to a specific nondegenerate recurrence.
- Stable mathematics does not eliminate representation limits or implementation errors.

## Further reading
- [MIT: convolution models and BIBO stability](https://web.mit.edu/6.02/www/s2012/handouts/11.pdf)
- [Julius O. Smith: one-pole stability](https://www.dsprelated.com/freebooks/filters/One_Pole.html)
- [NumPy: numerical scalar types and overflow](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/arrays.scalars.html)
- [SciPy: filtering and numerical recommendations](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.lfilter.html)

lessons.title: Process blocks without losing history
lessons.summary: Preserve filter state between blocks and separate computation deadlines from total latency.
lessons.body:
Devices and files often deliver samples in **processing blocks** rather than one at a time. A block boundary is a software boundary, not a break in the underlying signal. If coefficients, sample order and arithmetic stay the same, a sample-by-sample recurrence gives the same outputs regardless of how its input is divided into blocks, provided its **filter state** survives between them.

## Pass the state forward

This complete Python example processes the one-pole smoother with a previous-output weight of 0.5. The function accepts its initial state and returns its final state alongside the output list. It does not reset itself secretly.

```python
def smooth(block, state):
    output = []
    for sample in block:
        state = 0.5*sample + 0.5*state
        output.append(state)
    return output, state

x = [1.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0]
whole, _ = smooth(x, 0.0)
first, state = smooth(x[:2], 0.0)
second, state = smooth(x[2:], state)
assert whole == first + second
print(whole)
# [0.5, 0.75, 0.375, 0.1875]
```

Resetting the second block to zero produces two zeros there, losing the previous block's tail. This error often looks like a jump at every boundary. A direct FIR instead retains the required previous inputs; a library may store an equivalent transformed state. SciPy's `lfilter` exposes initial and final delay states as `zi` and `zf`. Retain its returned state in that API's representation; it is not generally just the last output sample.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: reading across pages
> Turning a page does not restart a story. You carry the relevant context into the next page.
>
> **How it maps:** Pages correspond to blocks; retained context corresponds to filter state. The amount printed on a page changes how the material is delivered, not its order or meaning.
>
> **Where it stops:** A digital filter needs a precisely defined finite state for these implementations, rather than a reader's flexible recollection.

## Decide what the end means

Zero state is one explicit startup policy. Another initial state may be justified by known earlier history. At the end of a finite recording, full convolution of an FIR can be obtained by appending enough zeros to flush the tail: one fewer zero than its number of taps. Keep only as many outputs as the chosen policy requires.

An IIR generally has no exact finite tail length. A finite application chooses a justified stopping tolerance or records a fixed additional duration. Do not flush with zeros between ordinary live blocks: the next block supplies the actual continuation. Startup, normal continuation and end-of-record handling are different decisions.

## A deadline is not total latency

For a regular incoming stream, one block's sample duration gives a recurring processing interval.

```formula
T_b = B / F_s
T_b = 64 / (48000 s^{−1})
T_b ≈ 0.001333 s
where
T_b: the duration represented by one block, in seconds (s)
B: the number of sample intervals per block, here 64
F_s: the sample rate, here 48000 sample intervals per second
s: second, the unit of time; s to the power minus one means per second
≈: approximately equal to; the result is rounded
In words: at 48000 samples per second, a new 64-sample block represents about 1.33 milliseconds of stream time.
```

In a simple single-worker pipeline, sustained processing must keep up with this arrival interval, with margin for other work and scheduling variation. A host timing test cannot guarantee a real device will meet every deadline.

End-to-end **latency** also includes collecting samples into buffers, queues, computation, filter delay and output hardware. Smaller blocks reduce some buffering delay but increase call overhead. State continuity establishes numerical correctness; timing measurements and a complete pipeline model address separate requirements.

## Key takeaways
- Retain state across normal blocks and use explicit startup and tail policies.
- Processing block size should not alter the recurrence's numerical result.
- Processing budget, filter delay and end-to-end latency measure different things.

## Further reading
- [SciPy: lfilter initial and final states](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.lfilter.html)
- [Smith: convolution and output length, Chapter 6](https://www.dspguide.com/CH6.PDF)
- [PortAudio: processing callbacks and bounded work](https://portaudio.com/docs/v19-doxydocs/writing_a_callback.html)
- [PortAudio: streams, buffers and buffering latency](https://portaudio.com/docs/v19-doxydocs/api_overview.html)
- [PortAudio: buffering, scheduling and timing model](https://github.com/PortAudio/portaudio/wiki/BufferingLatencyAndTimingImplementationGuidelines)

options.explanation: Correct. A simple worker needs enough processing capacity and margin to keep up, while total latency needs a broader model.

questions.workedExample:
Compute stream time represented by the block.

```formula
T_b = B / F_s
T_b = 64 / (48000 s^{−1})
T_b ≈ 0.001333 s
where
T_b: block duration in seconds (s)
B: block size of 64 sample intervals
F_s: rate of 48000 sample intervals per second
s: second; s to the power minus one means per second
≈: approximately equal to; the result is rounded
In words: a regular stream supplies another block about every one and one third milliseconds.
```

A deadline budget needs margin; end-to-end latency includes other stages.

questions.prompt: Which end-of-record and block-boundary policies are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Append flushing zeros between every live block
options.explanation: That inserts an artificial signal continuation before actual samples arrive and changes the output.

options.text: Flush a direct FIR at the final end using one fewer zero than its tap count
options.explanation: Correct. This exposes the finite full-convolution tail when later input is assumed zero.

options.text: Carry the library's returned state into the next normal block
options.explanation: Correct. The continuation must preserve state in the representation expected by that implementation.

options.text: Every IIR becomes exactly zero after the same fixed number of tail samples
options.explanation: An IIR generally has no exact finite tail; stopping requires a declared duration or tolerance.

questions.workedExample:
1. During a live stream, the next real block is the continuation, so preserve state without adding fictitious samples.
2. At a finite recording's end, choose whether to retain the tail.
3. Under a zero-after-record policy, a direct FIR needs one fewer flushing zero than its tap count to reveal its full tail.
4. An IIR typically needs an application-specific tail duration or tolerance rather than a universal exact length.
